questions.subtopic: 1D1 Fraud triangle, fraud risks and schemes. Fraud or error
questions.question: An internal auditor finds twelve duplicate supplier payments at a freight company. Which additional fact would most strongly point to fraud instead of error?

options.A: The duplicates exceed the amount set for reporting errors.
options.B: The clerk altered invoice numbers so the duplicate check passed.
options.C: The clerk knowingly skipped the duplicate check to clear a backlog.
options.D: The same clerk entered every one of the duplicate payments.

questions.key_concept: Fraud is a deliberate act marked by deceit, concealment or breach of trust for unfair advantage; a knowing shortcut without these is a control breach.
questions.pre_read: Two options describe deliberate acts. Ask which one also involves hiding something to gain an advantage.
questions.correct_explanation: The Standards' glossary treats fraud as a deliberate act marked by deceit, concealment or a similar breach of trust, carried out to gain an unfair or unlawful advantage. Altering invoice numbers to slip past a check is a chosen step to hide the payments. Knowingly skipping the check is the runner-up: it is deliberate, but it is an open shortcut with no deception and no gain, so it is a control breach, not fraud.

wrong_explanations.A: Size is not the test. The glossary's description of fraud sets no minimum amount, and a large duplicate can still be an honest mistake.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: skipping the check was deliberate, but intent alone is not fraud. Nothing was disguised and nobody gained; it is a breach of procedure.
wrong_explanations.D: One person behind every duplicate deserves a closer look, but repeated honest mistakes look the same. A pattern alone shows no deceit.

tips: Eliminate: A, because fraud has no minimum amount, and D, because one clerk's repeated entries could be honest mistakes.
Final two: B beats C because fraud needs deception for an advantage, not just a deliberate act; altered numbers conceal, a skipped check does not.
Exam cue: a deliberate act is not enough. Look for deceit or concealment aimed at an advantage before calling something a fraud indicator.

questions.subtopic: 1D1 Fraud triangle, fraud risks and schemes. The triangle side a control reaches
questions.question: An internal auditor notes that a clinic's cashier both records and pays refunds. Cashier pay was recently cut. Management plans to split the two tasks. Which fraud condition would that plan most directly reduce?

options.A: The motivation created by the recent cut in pay.
options.B: The rationalization that small refunds harm nobody.
options.C: The chance that two cashiers collude on refunds.
options.D: The opportunity to take cash unseen.

questions.key_concept: Dividing duties changes what one person is able to do alone, so of the fraud triangle's three conditions it bears on opportunity.
questions.pre_read: Name the three conditions of the fraud triangle first, then ask which one a change in who does what can alter.
questions.correct_explanation: The fraud triangle, as the CIA syllabus lists it, has three conditions: motivation, opportunity and rationalization. Splitting the two tasks changes what one cashier is able to do: nobody can now both record a refund and pay it out, so the chance to take cash unseen shrinks. That is opportunity. The pay cut is the runner-up because it is real, but splitting tasks changes what a person can do, not why they might want to.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the pay cut may add pressure or an excuse, but dividing tasks changes neither. It changes what one cashier can do unseen.
wrong_explanations.B: Rationalization is the excuse a person uses to feel justified. Changing who performs a task leaves that excuse exactly as it was.
wrong_explanations.C: Dividing tasks does not reduce collusion. Collusion is the weak point of the control, because two people acting together can still get past it.

tips: Eliminate: B, because an excuse lives in attitudes that task design does not touch, and C, because collusion is what defeats divided duties.
Final two: D beats A because separating duties removes the chance to act alone and unseen; the pay cut and its pressure stay unchanged.
Exam cue: on fraud triangle questions, ask what the change alters: what a person is able to do (opportunity), why they would, or how they excuse it.

questions.subtopic: 1D1 Fraud triangle, fraud risks and schemes. Fraud for the organization's benefit
questions.question: A sales director at a machinery maker bribes a customer's buyer to win an order. The director books the payment as marketing and gains nothing personally. How should an internal auditor best classify the act?

options.A: As fraud committed to gain an unlawful business advantage.
options.B: As a commercial decision outside the meaning of fraud.
options.C: As a recording error in the marketing expense account.
options.D: As a conflict of interest held by the sales director.

questions.key_concept: Fraud can be committed for the organization as well as against it: the advantage sought may be personal or for the business.
questions.pre_read: Notice who benefits from the act, then ask whether the meaning of fraud depends on who benefits.
questions.correct_explanation: The Standards' glossary treats fraud as a deliberate, deceptive act by a person or an organization to win an unfair or unlawful advantage, and that advantage can be personal or for the business. A hidden bribe booked as marketing fits. Calling it a commercial decision is the runner-up, but benefit to the company does not take an act out of the meaning of fraud.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: the company gains, yet the glossary's meaning of fraud covers an unlawful advantage for the business as well as for a person.
wrong_explanations.C: An error is unintended. The director chose to pay the buyer and to disguise the payment, so the wrong account is concealment, not a slip.
wrong_explanations.D: A conflict of interest is a competing interest that could sway a person's judgment. The director has none in this order; the deception is what matters here.

tips: Eliminate: C, because the mislabeled entry was deliberate, and D, because the director has no competing interest of their own in the order.
Final two: A beats B because the meaning of fraud covers an unlawful advantage for the organization, not only personal gain.
Exam cue: fraud can be committed for the organization as well as against it; who benefits does not decide the label.

questions.subtopic: 1D1 Fraud triangle, fraud risks and schemes. The fraud risk in the activity under review
questions.question: An internal auditor is planning an engagement on safety inspection records at an airline maintenance unit that pays bonuses for fast turnaround. Which fraud risk is most relevant to this engagement?

options.A: Turnaround targets that put mechanics under heavy pressure.
options.B: Tools and spare parts taken home by maintenance staff.
options.C: Inspection sign-offs falsified to protect turnaround bonuses.
options.D: Honest mistakes in inspection records made under bonus pressure.

questions.key_concept: A fraud risk is a deliberate deception for gain in the activity under review; information can be falsified as well as assets taken.
questions.pre_read: For each option ask two things: is it a deliberate act for gain, and does it sit in the records this engagement covers?
questions.correct_explanation: A fraud risk is a way someone could deliberately deceive for gain in the activity under review, which Standard 13.2 has every engagement consider. The glossary's description of fraud covers forgery and misuse of information as well as assets, and a speed bonus gives staff a reason to sign off inspections not done. Taking tools is the runner-up: it is fraud, but outside the inspection records this engagement covers.

wrong_explanations.A: Pressure from targets is a condition that makes fraud more likely, not a fraud risk in itself. The risk is the deliberate act the pressure may prompt.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: taking tools is a real fraud risk, but it concerns physical assets. This engagement covers inspection records, where the bonus rewards falsification.
wrong_explanations.D: A mistake made under bonus pressure is an error, because nothing is intended. The question asks for a fraud risk, which needs a deliberate act.

tips: Eliminate: A, because pressure is a condition and not a deliberate act, and D, because an honest mistake has no intent.
Final two: C beats B because the fraud risk to weigh sits in the activity under review; falsified records earn the bonus without any asset moving.
Exam cue: look for the fraud risk inside the activity under review; ask what could be falsified there and who would gain.

questions.subtopic: 1D2 Weighing fraud risk in an engagement. What planning must include on fraud
questions.question: An internal auditor has two days to plan an assurance engagement on a city's bus maintenance. Which planning step do the Standards most clearly require, however short the time?

options.A: Holding a fraud brainstorming session with the engagement team.
options.B: Reviewing the fraud risk assessment that fleet management prepared.
options.C: Considering specific fraud risks when identifying risks to review.
options.D: Plotting the engagement's risks on a likelihood and impact heat map.

questions.key_concept: Considering specific fraud risks in the engagement risk assessment is a requirement; brainstorming, heat maps and others' assessments are optional aids.
questions.pre_read: Sort the options into what the Standards say must be done and what they offer as helpful ways of doing it.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 13.2 Engagement Risk Assessment requires internal auditors, in every engagement, to consider specific fraud risks when identifying the risks to review. The other three are ways of doing that well, not requirements. Reviewing management's fraud risk assessment is the runner-up: the considerations to Standard 13.2 say such reviews may help, which makes it an option and not a must.

wrong_explanations.A: Brainstorming is sound practice for thinking through fraud scenarios, but the Standards do not require it. It is one way to meet the requirement.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: useful, and the considerations to Standard 13.2 mention it, but as something internal auditors may do when gathering information.
wrong_explanations.D: A heat map is an illustration the considerations mention for showing significance. The requirement is to evaluate and prioritize risks, not to draw them.

tips: Eliminate: A, because brainstorming is practice the Standards do not mention, and D, because a heat map is one optional way to show significance.
Final two: C beats B because considering fraud risk is a requirement in every engagement, while reviewing management's assessment is a 'may'.
Exam cue: when a question asks what the Standards require, separate the 'must' from the methods offered as 'should' or 'may'.

questions.subtopic: 1D2 Weighing fraud risk in an engagement. Advisory work and fraud risk
questions.question: Managers at a logistics firm ask an internal auditor for informal advice on a new expense app. The agreed terms exclude a written risk assessment. How should the auditor best handle fraud risk?

options.A: Weigh how the new app could enable fraud while preparing the advice.
options.B: Prepare a full documented fraud risk assessment before advising.
options.C: Leave fraud risk aside, in line with the agreed terms.
options.D: Ask the managers to amend the terms so fraud can be assessed.

questions.key_concept: In advisory work the agreement may remove the formal, documented risk assessment, but due professional care still weighs fraud.
questions.pre_read: Separate two things: whether fraud is thought about, and how formally that thinking has to be recorded.
questions.correct_explanation: Due professional care under Standard 4.2 includes weighing the chance of fraud in any service, advisory work included. Standard 13.2 adds that for advisory services a formal, written risk assessment may be unnecessary, depending on what was agreed, and here the agreed terms exclude one. Leaving fraud aside is the runner-up: the terms remove the document, not the thinking.

wrong_explanations.B: Standard 13.2 lets the agreement decide whether advisory work needs a formal, documented assessment, and these terms exclude one. This applies the assurance routine against them.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: the terms do exclude a written risk assessment, but Standard 4.2 still requires weighing the chance of fraud in every service.
wrong_explanations.D: No amendment is needed. Fraud can be weighed informally within the agreed terms; they rule out the formal document, not due professional care.

tips: Eliminate: B, because the agreed terms exclude a formal documented assessment, and D, because weighing fraud informally needs no change to the terms.
Final two: A beats C because the agreement can remove the written risk assessment for advisory work, but not the duty to weigh fraud.
Exam cue: in advisory work the formality of the risk assessment may drop by agreement; the thinking about fraud does not.

questions.subtopic: 1D2 Weighing fraud risk in an engagement. Ranking fraud risks by significance
questions.question: An internal auditor is planning an assurance engagement at a port authority. The auditor compares four processes for fraud risk, using the facts known at planning. Which process should the auditor rank as most significant for review?

options.A: Crane purchases of $8 million a year, each with three independent approvals.
options.B: Expense claims of $40,000 a year, with the most past errors.
options.C: Stationery orders of $15,000 a year, placed by one buyer alone.
options.D: Fee waivers of $8 million a year, granted by one clerk alone.

questions.key_concept: Fraud risks are prioritized by significance, which combines how likely the fraud is with how much harm it would do.
questions.pre_read: For each risk, note the amount at stake and how easily one person could act unseen. A ranking has to combine the two.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 13.2 requires risks to be evaluated for significance and prioritized; the glossary says significance is typically judged by impact and likelihood. Fee waivers and crane purchases put the same amount at stake, so impact does not separate them. One clerk can grant a waiver alone, which makes fraud there more likely. Crane purchases are the runner-up: their three approvals are untested, so they stay in the review, but nothing known ranks them higher.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the amount at stake is the same, and the three approvals are still untested, so this risk stays in the review. Nothing known ranks it above the waivers.
wrong_explanations.B: Past errors are not fraud, and the amounts are small. A history of honest mistakes says little about how likely or costly a deliberate act would be.
wrong_explanations.C: One buyer acting alone makes fraud likely, but $15,000 a year caps the impact. Significance needs both halves.

tips: Eliminate: B, because past errors are not evidence of fraud and the amounts are small, and C, because a small amount limits impact however weak the control.
Final two: D beats A because the amounts are equal and one clerk can act alone; untested approvals keep crane purchases in the review but do not rank them higher.
Exam cue: rank fraud exposure on impact and likelihood together, using the facts known. A control described at planning still has to be assessed and tested in the engagement.

questions.subtopic: 1D2 Weighing fraud risk in an engagement. Updating an earlier risk assessment
questions.question: An internal auditor plans a repeat engagement on repairs contracts at a housing association, where last year's risk assessment rated fraud risk low. Which of the following best states the minimum the Standards require?

options.A: Reuse last year's assessment exactly as it stands this year.
options.B: Review and update last year's assessment for this engagement.
options.C: Build a new assessment and set last year's work aside.
options.D: Update last year's assessment where management reports a change.

questions.key_concept: For an activity assessed in an earlier engagement, the requirement is a review and update of that risk assessment: no less, and no more.
questions.pre_read: The question asks for the minimum that still meets the requirement. Check each option for doing less, or more, than that.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 13.2 says that when the relevant risks of an activity were identified in an earlier engagement, a review and update of that assessment is all that is required. That is the minimum: staff, systems and pressures change in a year, and a low rating is not permanent. Reusing the assessment untouched is the runner-up, but it falls below the requirement.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the earlier work can be used, but not untouched. The requirement is to review and update it, and a low rating can change.
wrong_explanations.C: A new assessment meets the requirement but is more than the minimum. For an activity assessed before, review and update is enough.
wrong_explanations.D: The review is the internal auditors' own. Updating what management reports and nothing else leaves the rest unreviewed, which is less than the requirement.

tips: Eliminate: C, because rebuilding is more than the minimum, and D, because the internal auditors review the assessment themselves instead of waiting for management's reports.
Final two: B beats A because the minimum is review and update; reuse without review assumes nothing changed, including the fraud risks.
Exam cue: for a repeat engagement, the earlier risk assessment is a starting point to review and update, not to copy or discard.

questions.subtopic: 1D3 Fraud risk management and red flags. A missing fraud response plan
questions.question: An internal auditor is evaluating fraud risk management at a dairy cooperative. The auditor finds a hotline and an anti-fraud policy, but nothing stating who investigates a report. Which recommendation is most important?

options.A: That management define roles in a fraud response plan.
options.B: That the hotline vendor investigate the reports it receives.
options.C: That senior management decide case by case who investigates.
options.D: That internal audit lead the investigation of hotline reports.

questions.key_concept: An organization should have a fraud response plan saying who does what when fraud is suspected; adopting it is management's job.
questions.pre_read: Find the gap in the program first, then ask who should close it and when.
questions.correct_explanation: The IIA's position paper on fraud says an organization should have a fraud response plan that sets out its policies and investigation methods and makes internal audit's role clear when fraud is suspected. The plan is management's to adopt, in advance. Deciding case by case is the runner-up: management stays in charge, but roles are still unsettled when a report arrives.

wrong_explanations.B: A hotline vendor receives reports. Investigating needs people with the right skills and the organization's authority, which a response plan would assign.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: it keeps the decision with management, but deciding each time is the gap itself. The position paper calls for a plan set in advance.
wrong_explanations.D: Investigating is not normally internal audit's task. It depends on the mandate and on having the specific skills, which the plan should make clear.

tips: Eliminate: B, because receiving reports is not the same as being equipped to investigate them, and D, because internal audit investigates where mandate and skills allow.
Final two: A beats C because management should settle who responds before a case arises; case-by-case choices leave the gap open.
Exam cue: a policy and a hotline are not a full program; look for a response plan that says who does what when fraud is suspected.

questions.subtopic: 1D3 Fraud risk management and red flags. Internal audit's part in managing fraud risk
questions.question: An internal auditor is asked to correct a draft anti-fraud policy at a rail operator. Which statement best describes the internal audit function's part in managing fraud risk?

options.A: It prevents fraud in day-to-day operations and reports fraud to the board.
options.B: It assesses anti-fraud controls and must audit fraud every year.
options.C: It investigates each fraud report and audits fraud every year.
options.D: It assesses anti-fraud controls and considers fraud risk in its plan.

questions.key_concept: Management prevents fraud; internal audit assesses the anti-fraud controls, and its plan must consider coverage of fraud risk.
questions.pre_read: Each statement has two halves. Test each half against who owns prevention and against what the plan is required to do.
questions.correct_explanation: The IIA's position paper on fraud gives internal audit the role of assessing the controls that prevent and detect fraud; prevention itself is management's responsibility. Standard 9.4 requires the internal audit plan to consider coverage of fraud risk. The yearly fraud audit is the runner-up: it sounds diligent, but considering coverage is the requirement, and that does not mean a dedicated fraud audit each year.

wrong_explanations.A: Preventing fraud in operations is management's responsibility. The position paper says it is not a direct duty of internal audit, which assesses the controls.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: the first half is right, but Standard 9.4 requires the plan to consider coverage of fraud risk, not a fraud audit every year.
wrong_explanations.C: Investigating is not normally internal audit's task; it depends on mandate and skills. A yearly fraud audit is not a requirement either.

tips: Eliminate: A, because prevention in operations belongs to management, and C, because internal audit investigates where mandate and skills allow.
Final two: D beats B because Standard 9.4 asks the plan to consider coverage of fraud risk; it sets no yearly fraud audit.
Exam cue: management prevents and responds; internal audit assesses the controls and considers fraud risk in its plan and each engagement.

questions.subtopic: 1D3 Fraud risk management and red flags. Testing an explanation for a red flag
questions.question: At a tea exporter, the warehouse manager tells an internal auditor that stock write-offs tripled because of monsoon damage. Which evidence would best test that explanation?

options.A: A statement of the cause, signed by the warehouse manager.
options.B: Local rainfall records and the auditor's inspection of the damaged stock.
options.C: Write-off forms completed and signed by the warehouse supervisors.
options.D: The auditor's own recount of the stock still held in the warehouse.

questions.key_concept: Evidence must be relevant to the claim as well as reliable: first-hand evidence that bears on another question does not test the explanation.
questions.pre_read: For each piece of evidence, ask two things: who produced it, and whether it bears on the cause the manager gave.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 14.1 asks for information that is relevant as well as reliable, and Standard 4.3 Professional Skepticism has internal auditors test statements that may be incomplete. Rainfall records come from outside and the inspection is first-hand, and both bear on the stated cause: monsoon damage. The auditor's recount is the runner-up: equally first-hand, but it shows how much stock is left, not why the rest was written off.

wrong_explanations.A: A signed statement repeats the explanation in writing. The source is the person whose account is being tested, so it corroborates nothing.
wrong_explanations.C: The manager's own staff prepared the forms. They show what was recorded as written off, not whether monsoon damage caused it.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: a recount is first-hand and reliable, but it answers a different question. It confirms how much stock remains, not what caused the write-offs.

tips: Eliminate: A, because a signature repeats the same person's claim, and C, because the manager's own staff prepared the forms.

questions.subtopic: 1D3 Fraud risk management and red flags. A red flag that involves senior management
questions.question: The chief audit executive (CAE) of a credit union learns that the chief operating officer had staff backdate loan approvals. No policy or procedure covers concerns about executives. Who should best receive the CAE's report?

options.A: The chief executive officer, who supervises the chief operating officer.
options.B: The head of compliance, who oversees the code of conduct.
options.C: The board of directors, through its audit committee.
options.D: The external auditor that reviews the loan book.

questions.key_concept: Concerns are reported as policy directs; where senior management is involved and no policy sets the route, the chief audit executive should tell the board.
questions.pre_read: Note the rank of the person involved and what the stem says about policy, then ask who oversees that person.
questions.correct_explanation: The considerations to Standard 1.2 say that when a member of senior management has acted against the organization's ethical expectations, the chief audit executive should report it to the board. A chief operating officer is senior management, and no policy or procedure here sets another route. The chief executive officer is the runner-up: senior to the person involved and able to act, but the Standards name the board for conduct at this level.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the chief executive officer can act, but for conduct by a member of senior management the Standard 1.2 considerations name the board.
wrong_explanations.B: No policy or procedure here covers executives, and compliance is a management function. For senior management's conduct the Standards' considerations point to the board.
wrong_explanations.D: External auditors are not the organization's channel for ethics concerns. Reports outside the organization follow what laws, regulations and policies specify.

tips: Eliminate: B, because a management function is not the route for conduct by senior management, and D, because outside parties are told as law and policy specify.
Final two: C beats A because the Standards' considerations send a senior management matter to the board; this is a 'should', and no policy or procedure here says otherwise.
Exam cue: check the policy first, then who is involved. A route that policy sets is the must; for senior management with no route set, expect the board.

questions.subtopic: 1D4 Controls that prevent and detect fraud. Telling a detective control from a preventive one
questions.question: An internal auditor is classifying an electronics retailer's refund controls in a risk and control matrix. Which control should the auditor most appropriately record as detective?

options.A: A system limit that blocks refunds above a set amount.
options.B: A rule that different staff enter and pay refunds.
options.C: A supervisor's approval before a refund is paid out.
options.D: A supervisor's weekly review of refunds already paid.

questions.key_concept: Timing decides the type: a control that acts before the transaction completes prevents; one that looks afterward detects.
questions.pre_read: For each control, ask when it acts: before the refund is paid, or after.
questions.correct_explanation: A detective control finds a problem after it has happened. A weekly look at refunds already paid can reveal an improper refund only afterward; the CIA syllabus lists supervisory reviews among controls that detect fraud. The supervisor's approval before payment is the runner-up: the same person and a similar check, but it comes first, so it works as an authority level that prevents.

wrong_explanations.A: A system limit stops an oversized refund before it is paid. Stopping the event beforehand makes the control preventive.
wrong_explanations.B: Dividing entry and payment between different people removes the chance to act alone before any refund goes out, so it is preventive.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: it involves a supervisor's check, but approval comes before payment. An authorization that can stop the transaction is preventive.

tips: Eliminate: A, because a blocking limit acts before the refund is paid, and B, because divided duties also work before the event.
Final two: D beats C because timing decides the type: approval before payment prevents, while review after payment detects.
Exam cue: ask when the control acts. Before the transaction completes it prevents; afterward it detects.

questions.subtopic: 1D4 Controls that prevent and detect fraud. A gap that detection cannot close
questions.question: At a cement distributor, supplier payments cannot be recalled once released, and the fraud controls are a monthly reconciliation and a hotline. Which control should an internal auditor recommend adding as most important?

options.A: A daily reconciliation in place of the monthly one.
options.B: Approval at a set authority level before release.
options.C: A supervisor's weekly review of released payments.
options.D: Wider promotion of the hotline to the payments staff.

questions.key_concept: When a loss cannot be undone, detection comes too late: the gap needs a control that acts before the transaction, such as an authority level.
questions.pre_read: Ask when each control acts, and whether that moment is early enough for a payment that cannot be recalled.
questions.correct_explanation: A reconciliation and a hotline are among the controls the CIA syllabus lists as detecting fraud: they act after the event. For a payment that cannot be recalled, that is after the loss. The syllabus names authority levels as a way to prevent fraud, and approval before release acts in time. A daily reconciliation is the runner-up: faster, but still after the money has gone.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: it finds a false payment sooner, but still after release. For money that cannot be recalled, quicker detection leaves the gap.
wrong_explanations.C: A supervisor's review of released payments is a detective control. Like the reconciliation, it reports the loss after it has happened.
wrong_explanations.D: A hotline brings concerns to light after someone notices them. Promoting it adds to detection, which the process already has, not prevention.

tips: Eliminate: C, because a review of released payments acts after the loss, and D, because a hotline is also a detective control.
Final two: B beats A because approval before release can stop the payment; a daily reconciliation shortens the time until the loss is found.
Exam cue: match the control's timing to the risk. Where a loss cannot be reversed, look for the control that acts before the transaction.

questions.subtopic: 1D4 Controls that prevent and detect fraud. Segregation of duties in a small team
questions.question: An aid charity's field office has two officers. One orders, receives and records fuel vouchers. The other is away on site visits most days and cannot take deliveries. What is the internal auditor's best recommendation?

options.A: Management has the second officer review voucher records each week.
options.B: Internal audit approves voucher orders until staffing improves.
options.C: The first officer certifies each month that no vouchers were misused.
options.D: Management moves the receiving of vouchers to the second officer.

questions.key_concept: Where duties cannot be separated, management adds an independent check; the internal auditor recommends it and does not operate it.
questions.pre_read: Ask who would check the officer's work under each option, whether that person can do it, and whether that person is management.
questions.correct_explanation: Controls are management's to design and run, and the IIA's position paper on fraud gives internal audit the role of assessing them. The second officer cannot take deliveries, so receiving cannot be split off, but a weekly review gives someone else sight of the vouchers. Internal audit approving orders is the runner-up: it adds a second person, but it makes the auditor part of the process to be assessed later.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: a second person does check each order, but approving transactions is a management responsibility. The auditor could not later assess that process objectively.
wrong_explanations.C: A person who could misuse vouchers cannot be the check on their own work. A control over one officer needs someone independent of that officer.
wrong_explanations.D: Splitting receiving from ordering would be the natural fix, but the stem says the second officer, away on site visits most days, cannot take deliveries.

tips: Eliminate: C, because a check must be independent of the person checked, and D, because the stem says the second officer cannot take deliveries.
Final two: A beats B because management operates controls; an internal auditor who approves transactions takes on management's job and loses objectivity over it.
Exam cue: when duties cannot be separated, look for an independent review run by management, not by the internal auditor.

questions.subtopic: 1D4 Controls that prevent and detect fraud. Tone at the top and the likelihood of fraud
questions.question: An internal auditor finds that executives at a lender routinely waive approval limits for favored clients, although all staff signed the code of conduct. How should the auditor best reflect this when assessing engagement risks?

options.A: As a fraud risk to rate once testing shows an actual loss.
options.B: As a management prerogative outside the risk assessment.
options.C: As a condition that raises the rated likelihood of fraud.
options.D: As a fraud risk the signed code of conduct reduces to low.

questions.key_concept: Tone at the top is judged by what leaders do; leaders who set controls aside raise the likelihood of fraud.
questions.pre_read: Compare what the written rules say with what the leaders do, and ask which one staff will follow.
questions.correct_explanation: Tone at the top shows in what leaders do, and the CIA syllabus ties it to the likelihood of fraud. Executives who set controls aside signal that rules bend. Due professional care under Standard 4.2 includes weighing how probable fraud is, and this conduct makes it more probable. Relying on the signed code is the runner-up, but a code states intent; behavior at the top that contradicts it weakens the code.

wrong_explanations.A: Fraud risk is weighed during planning so that it can shape the tests. Waiting for a loss means the engagement was planned without it.
wrong_explanations.B: Leaders can change limits through proper channels. Routinely setting them aside for favored clients is override, which belongs in the engagement risk assessment.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: a signed code is a real control, but it shows intent. Leaders who set limits aside weaken it, so it cannot rate the risk low.

tips: Eliminate: A, because fraud risk is rated in planning and not after a loss appears, and B, because override by leaders is itself a risk to assess.
Final two: C beats D because tone is judged by leaders' actions; a signed code cannot offset executives who set controls aside.
Exam cue: when written ethics rules and leaders' behavior disagree, weigh the behavior; it raises the likelihood of fraud.

questions.subtopic: 1D5 Fraud investigation techniques and roles. What decides internal audit's investigation role
questions.question: After a hotline report alleges tuition fee theft at a university, the board asks whether internal audit should investigate. Which consideration most determines the internal audit function's role?

options.A: Its independence from the managers of the university's fee office.
options.B: Its mandate and its competencies for investigative work.
options.C: The size and sensitivity of the alleged loss.
options.D: The objectivity of the internal auditors who would be assigned.

questions.key_concept: Whether internal audit investigates depends on its mandate and on having, or obtaining, the competencies; it is not automatic.
questions.pre_read: Ask two questions of each option: does it give authority to investigate, and does it give the skill?
questions.correct_explanation: Two things decide the role. The mandate comes first: the considerations to Standard 6.1 give investigations as an example of a service a charter may name. And Standard 3.1 requires internal auditors to take on only services they have, or can obtain, the competencies for. Independence is the runner-up: it helps credibility, but it supplies neither authority nor investigative skill.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: independence matters for credibility, but it gives neither the authority nor the skill to investigate. Those come from the mandate and competencies.
wrong_explanations.C: The size and sensitivity of the loss affect urgency and resourcing, not whether investigating falls within internal audit's role.
wrong_explanations.D: Objectivity matters when choosing who is assigned. It does not give the function authority to investigate or the skills to do it.

tips: Eliminate: C, because the size of the loss shapes urgency and not the role, and D, because objectivity is about who is assigned, not about authority or skill.
Final two: B beats A because independence does not make an investigator; the mandate grants the role and competencies make it safe to perform.
Exam cue: asked whether internal audit investigates fraud, test two things: is it in the mandate, and are the competencies there?

questions.subtopic: 1D5 Fraud investigation techniques and roles. Competencies before investigative work
questions.question: A utility's internal audit charter lists investigations, but the function has no trained investigator and cannot fund one. Management asks internal audit to investigate a meter-reading fraud. How should the chief audit executive best respond?

options.A: Accept, and assign the function's two most experienced auditors.
options.B: Accept under the charter, and tell the board about the skills gap.
options.C: Decline, and ask the board to drop investigations from the charter.
options.D: Decline to lead it, and report the skills gap to the board.

questions.key_concept: Internal auditors take on only services they have, or can obtain, the competencies for; a gap in a charter service is reported to the board.
questions.pre_read: The stem settles two things: the charter's authority, and whether the skills can be obtained. Ask which one decides.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 3.1 limits internal auditors to services they have, or can obtain, the competencies for. The charter gives authority, but here the skills are neither held nor obtainable, so the function should not lead; the IIA's position paper on fraud says investigations are best left to experienced people. Standard 8.2 Resources has the board told of a resource shortfall. Accepting under the charter is the runner-up: telling the board does not supply the skill.

wrong_explanations.A: Audit experience is not investigative competence. The stem says the function has no trained investigator, so seniority does not close the gap.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: the charter authorizes the service and the board should hear of the gap, but the competencies must be held or obtainable before the work is accepted.
wrong_explanations.C: Changing the charter is the board's decision, not a reply to this request. Standards 3.1 and 8.2 have the chief audit executive seek the missing skills and report the shortfall.

tips: Eliminate: A, because seniority in auditing is not investigative skill, and C, because a missing skill is reported and sought before anyone rewrites the charter.
Final two: D beats B because Standard 3.1 bars services the function cannot become competent to perform; telling the board about the gap does not supply the skill.

Exam cue: mandate answers 'may we?', competency answers 'can we?'. If the skills cannot be obtained, decline, say who should do the work, and report the funding gap to the board and senior management.

questions.subtopic: 1D5 Fraud investigation techniques and roles. Using investigators' information in planning
questions.question: An internal auditor is planning an engagement on an airline's baggage claims. The investigations unit closed six cases of claims fraud last year. What is the auditor's best use of that information?

options.A: Rely on the unit's casework as assurance over claims controls.
options.B: Treat the cases as optional background outside the risk assessment.
options.C: Use the case patterns in assessing the engagement's fraud risks.
options.D: Share the case details with the claims manager before fieldwork.

questions.key_concept: Investigators' past cases, trends and complaints are planning input: they show where a process has been exposed to fraud.
questions.pre_read: Ask what six closed cases say about the process, and what the investigators did and did not examine.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 13.2 requires specific fraud risks to be considered when an engagement's risks are identified, and six cases in this process show which schemes were tried and which controls failed. Its considerations add that auditors may draw on others' risk work, and the CIA syllabus names prior investigations and trends. Relying on the casework as assurance is the runner-up, but investigators examined six cases, not whether claims controls work.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the unit's work is relevant, but it examined specific cases. It gave no assurance that claims controls now work, and six cases signal exposure.
wrong_explanations.B: Reviewing others' work is a 'may', but these cases are already known. Considering specific fraud risks is a requirement, and the cases point straight at them.
wrong_explanations.D: Investigation details are confidential and are shared as policy and law allow. Planning needs the patterns; the manager has no need for the files.

tips: Eliminate: B, because known fraud cases bear on a requirement and are not optional reading, and D, because investigation details are protected information.
Final two: C beats A because investigators examined individual cases; their findings inform the risk assessment and do not replace assurance over the process.
Exam cue: investigators' risk assessments, past cases, trends and complaints are planning input for the internal auditor.

questions.subtopic: 1D5 Fraud investigation techniques and roles. Internal audit's part after a fraud
questions.question: An outside forensic firm has finished investigating a payroll fraud at a hotel group and reported to the board. What is the internal audit function's most appropriate contribution now?

options.A: Assess how the payroll controls failed and recommend improvements.
options.B: Put stronger payroll controls in place before the next pay run.
options.C: Assure the board that no similar fraud exists in other units.
options.D: Repeat the whole investigation to confirm the forensic firm's findings.

questions.key_concept: After a fraud, internal audit works out how the controls failed and recommends improvements; management implements them.
questions.pre_read: Sort the options by who should act, and by whether anyone could truthfully deliver what the option promises.
questions.correct_explanation: The IIA's position paper on fraud gives internal audit a part once a fraud has happened: it should work out how the controls failed, point to improvements, and consider whether similar problems are likely elsewhere. Acting on the recommendations is management's work. Putting new controls in place is the runner-up: the right goal, but done by the wrong party, and it would leave internal audit assessing its own work.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: stronger controls are needed, but management designs and operates them. An internal auditor who installs controls cannot later assess them objectively.
wrong_explanations.C: Internal audit should consider whether similar problems are likely elsewhere, but assurance is not a guarantee. Nobody can promise that no fraud exists.
wrong_explanations.D: Qualified specialists have investigated and reported. Redoing their work adds cost without a reason to doubt it, and it is not internal audit's part.

tips: Eliminate: C, because no assurance can promise the absence of fraud, and D, because a completed specialist investigation is not redone without cause.
Final two: A beats B because internal audit assesses and recommends, while management implements; the auditor who builds a control cannot assess it later.
Exam cue: after a fraud, internal audit asks how the controls failed and what should improve; management fixes and disciplines.

questions.subtopic: 1D1 Fraud triangle, fraud risks and schemes. Rationalization among four staff remarks
questions.question: An internal auditor is planning a payroll engagement at a cashmere exporter and notes four remarks from staff interviews. Which of the following remarks best shows the fraud triangle condition of rationalization?

options.A: A clerk says two colleagues are struggling to repay loans.
options.B: A clerk says nobody else looks at the hours they enter.
options.C: A clerk says rounding hours up only takes back what is owed.
options.D: A clerk says approved overtime has doubled in three months.

questions.key_concept: The fraud triangle has three conditions: motivation, opportunity and rationalization. Rationalization is the excuse that makes the act seem acceptable to the person.
questions.pre_read: Sort each remark first: a reason to want money, a chance to take it, an excuse for taking it, or a sign something happened.
questions.correct_explanation: The CIA syllabus lists three fraud triangle conditions: motivation, opportunity and rationalization. To rationalize is to give oneself a reason that makes an act feel acceptable, and 'only takes back what is owed' is such an excuse. The loan trouble is the runner-up: it shows money pressure, which is a reason to want the gain (motivation), not a justification for taking it.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: debts the clerks cannot repay are money pressure. That is a reason to want more pay, which is motivation, not an excuse for taking it.
wrong_explanations.B: Hours that nobody else looks at are a gap that lets false hours pass unseen. That describes opportunity.
wrong_explanations.D: A jump in approved hours is a red flag that something may have happened. It is an indicator to examine, not one of the three conditions.

tips: Eliminate: B, because hours that nobody else checks describe opportunity, and D, because a jump in hours is a red flag and not a condition.
Final two: C beats A because rationalization is the excuse a person gives for the act, while money pressure is the reason to want the gain.
Exam cue: for a fraud triangle fact, ask whether it is a reason to want, a chance to take, or an excuse to justify. Hardship explains wanting; an excuse claims the taking is fair.

questions.subtopic: 1D1 Fraud triangle, fraud risks and schemes. Information taken but not yet used
questions.question: A sales manager leaving a software firm admits copying the firm's client list under renamed files. The manager admits planning to use the list at a competitor. The list is still unused. How should an internal auditor best classify the act?

options.A: As fraud committed through taking the firm's information.
options.B: As a fraud risk that the firm should now assess.
options.C: As a data handling error that deletion will correct.
options.D: As a confidentiality breach that falls short of fraud.

questions.key_concept: The glossary's fraud covers taking information as well as assets; the advantage has to be sought by a deliberate, concealed act, not yet obtained.
questions.pre_read: Check three things the glossary looks for: was the act deliberate, was it hidden, and what was it meant to secure?
questions.correct_explanation: The Standards' glossary treats fraud as a deliberate act with marks such as concealment or the taking of assets or information, aimed at an unfair advantage, personal or for a business. Copying the list under renamed files for use at a competitor fits each part. A fraud risk is the runner-up, but a risk is something that might happen; this act has happened, and the advantage only has to be sought, not obtained.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: nothing has been gained yet, but a fraud risk is a possibility. Here the deliberate, concealed act has happened; the glossary asks what it was meant to secure.
wrong_explanations.C: An error is unintended. The manager admits renaming the files and copying the list for use at a competitor, so the act was deliberate and concealed.
wrong_explanations.D: It does break confidentiality rules, but the label stops short: the glossary's fraud includes taking information by concealment to gain an unfair advantage.

tips: Eliminate: C, because an error is unintended and the manager admits the purpose, and D, because the glossary's fraud covers information taken by concealment for an advantage.
Final two: A beats B because a fraud risk is a possibility, and here the deliberate, hidden act has already taken place; the advantage only has to be sought, not obtained.
Exam cue: to test for fraud, look for intent, concealment and an unfair advantage sought. Loss, amount and whether the plan succeeded do not decide it.

questions.subtopic: 1D2 Weighing fraud risk in an engagement. A test that fits the fraud scenario
questions.question: Internal auditors at a water bottler imagine a fraud scheme. A buyer approves small payments alone and pays a supplier that exists only on paper. The supplier's account and address are the buyer's own. Which test best reveals the scheme?

options.A: Confirming balances by letter sent to each supplier's address.
options.B: Checking paid invoices for invoice numbers that repeat.
options.C: Listing the payments just under the buyer's approval limit.
options.D: Comparing the suppliers' bank details with staff records.

questions.key_concept: A fraud test has to reach past records the fraudster controls: evidence is more reliable when its source is independent of the people involved.
questions.pre_read: For each test, ask what it would show and who would supply the evidence it relies on. Is that source independent of the buyer?
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 13.6 builds the work program on the risk assessment, so the scenario picks the test: the supplier's account is the buyer's own, and staff records, which the buyer does not keep, hold it. Standard 14.1 explains why the runner-up fails. A confirmation is strong evidence when the party replying is independent, but this letter goes to the buyer's own address, so the buyer would answer it.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: a third party's confirmation is normally reliable, but this letter goes to the buyer's own address. The reply would come from the buyer, not an independent party.
wrong_explanations.B: Repeated invoice numbers point to double billing. A paper supplier can give each false invoice its own number, so this check shows nothing.
wrong_explanations.C: Payments just under the limit show what the buyer approved alone, genuine purchases included. They do not show that the supplier behind a payment is unreal.

tips: Eliminate: B, because repeated invoice numbers reveal double billing and not a supplier that does not exist, and C, because payments under the limit include genuine purchases.
Final two: D beats A because a confirmation is only as independent as the party replying; here the letter goes to the buyer's own address.
Exam cue: when choosing a fraud test, ask how the scheme would be hidden, then pick evidence the person hiding it cannot create or control.

questions.subtopic: 1D3 Fraud risk management and red flags. A red flag with an innocent explanation
questions.question: A flower exporter's policy requires write-offs to be approved within 30 days. An internal auditor finds 14 write-offs still unapproved after four months. The insurer's records confirm each loss was genuine. How should the auditor best treat these write-offs?

options.A: Report them to the chief audit executive as suspected fraud.
options.B: Evaluate the overdue approvals as a potential finding.
options.C: Close the matter, as the insurer's records answer the concern.
options.D: Evaluate the scale of stock losses as a potential finding.

questions.key_concept: A red flag that evidence explains is no longer a fraud concern, but any gap between policy and practice is still a potential finding.
questions.pre_read: Two questions sit in this stem: were the losses real, and was the approval rule followed? Answer each one separately.
questions.correct_explanation: Under Standard 14.2, when what the auditor observes differs from the criteria, the gap is a potential finding to evaluate. The one criterion here is the 30-day rule, and approvals four months overdue break it. The insurer's records answer the fraud worry, since the losses were real. Closing the matter is the runner-up: it is right about fraud and wrong about the control, because nobody reviewed the write-offs when policy said they should.

wrong_explanations.A: Standard 4.3 had the auditor seek more evidence, and the insurer's independent records show the losses were real, so nothing points to deceit. Calling it suspected fraud overstates the evidence.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: the fraud concern is answered, but the 30-day approval rule was still broken. That gap is a potential finding in its own right.
wrong_explanations.D: A finding is a gap between a criterion and what the auditor observes. No limit on stock losses is given here; the rule that was broken is the 30-day approval.

tips: Eliminate: A, because independent evidence shows the losses were real, and D, because the facts give no criterion that the losses themselves broke.
Final two: B beats C because a finding is a gap between criteria and condition; the 30-day policy was broken whether or not anyone committed fraud.
Exam cue: clearing a red flag answers 'was it fraud?'. Ask separately 'did the control work?'. A no to the second is still a potential finding.

questions.subtopic: 1D3 Fraud risk management and red flags. Support that cannot be produced
questions.question: An internal auditor is testing 60 contractor payments at a road agency. The files for 12 payments were lost in an office move and cannot be rebuilt. What do the Standards most clearly require?

options.A: Deciding whether the missing support is itself a finding.
options.B: Testing 12 further payments chosen by the same method.
options.C: Rating the controls over contractor payments as ineffective.
options.D: Concluding on the 48 payments whose files were available.

questions.key_concept: When support an auditor needs does not exist, the auditor must decide whether its absence is itself a finding: missing files are information.
questions.pre_read: Missing documents are a common process red flag. Ask what the Standards say about evidence that cannot be obtained at all.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 14.1 covers this case: where needed evidence is not obtainable, the internal auditor must judge whether that fact is itself a finding. Missing files are also a red flag. Testing 12 more is the runner-up: the same standard lets the auditor gather more, but that is a choice and leaves the lost files unexplained. Where the gap stops planned tests, Standard 13.3 treats it as a scope limitation to discuss with management.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: Standard 14.1 has the auditor decide whether to gather more, so extra items may be tested. That is optional and does not answer for the 12 lost files.
wrong_explanations.C: Lost files show that support is missing for 12 payments. They do not show how approval or payment controls performed, so this conclusion outruns the evidence.
wrong_explanations.D: No standard requires this. A conclusion on 48 that is silent about the 12 overstates the work; Standard 13.3 has a scope limitation discussed with management.

tips: Eliminate: C, because lost files alone do not show how the payment controls performed, and D, because a conclusion on 48 that is silent about the 12 overstates the work.
Final two: A beats B because testing more items is a choice that answers a different question; the Standards require a decision on the support that cannot be obtained.
Exam cue: when support cannot be produced, do not work around it. On CIA questions the internal auditor usually asks whether the absence itself should be reported.

questions.subtopic: 1D4 Controls that prevent and detect fraud. A scheme the records do not show
questions.question: A fishery's stores clerk suspects the buyer and a supplier of inflating prices for shared gain, though every record matches the contract. Which control would an internal auditor rate most likely to expose this?

options.A: The monthly reconciliation of supplier statements to the ledger.
options.B: The supervisor's weekly review of orders against their contracts.
options.C: The approval limit that sends larger orders to a director.
options.D: The whistleblower hotline that the audit committee oversees.

questions.key_concept: Hotlines, reconciliations and supervisory reviews all detect fraud; none outranks the others. Which one exposes a scheme depends on where the stem puts the knowledge.
questions.pre_read: Ask what each control looks at, then find where the stem puts the knowledge of the scheme.
questions.correct_explanation: The CIA syllabus lists hotlines, reconciliations and supervisory reviews as controls that detect fraud, and authority levels as preventing it. The syllabus ranks none of them, so the stem decides: a reconciliation compares records, a review looks at the orders put before the supervisor, and a hotline carries what a person knows. Here the records match and only a clerk suspects. The supervisor's review is the runner-up, but these orders match their contracts.

wrong_explanations.A: A reconciliation compares two records and follows up differences. Supplier statements and the ledger agree here, because the inflated prices were invoiced and recorded consistently.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: this review sets orders beside their contracts, and the stem says every record matches the contract. The supervisor would see nothing unusual.
wrong_explanations.C: An approval limit is a control that prevents: it acts before an order is placed. It does not bring to light a scheme in orders that already match their contracts.

tips: Eliminate: A, because the supplier statements and the ledger agree, and C, because an approval limit acts before an order is placed and does not expose one already made.
Final two: D beats B because the stem leaves every record matching the contract, so the review of orders sees nothing unusual; the one person who suspects needs a route to report.
Exam cue: the syllabus classes these controls as detecting fraud and ranks none. To choose among them, find where the stem puts the difference, the oddity or the knowledge.

questions.subtopic: 1D5 Fraud investigation techniques and roles. A misleading remark in a fact-finding interview
questions.question: An internal auditor wants a stores clerk to think that the supervisor has explained missing stock. The auditor plans to say 'your supervisor already talked to us'. That talk was only about a roster query. Which view is most accurate?

options.A: Proper: an auditor may choose which facts to share.
options.B: Proper: the test is whether each word said is accurate.
options.C: Improper: the test is what the clerk is led to believe.
options.D: Improper: the clerk is owed the material facts the auditor has.

questions.key_concept: Honesty is more than accuracy: an internal auditor must not use a statement, even a literally correct one, to mislead the person hearing it.
questions.pre_read: Two tests are in play: is each word accurate, and what is the listener meant to believe? Ask which one the Standards apply.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 1.1 leaves no room for a useful deception: what an internal auditor tells people may not mislead them, and doubting someone's account does not change that. Standard 4.3 adds that a skeptical auditor asks about what does not add up plainly and honestly. The remark is accurate, yet it is chosen to plant a false belief. Accuracy is the runner-up: it is necessary, but a statement can be accurate and still deceive.

wrong_explanations.A: An auditor need not tell an interviewee everything, but holding facts back is not the plan. The remark is chosen so the clerk believes something that did not happen.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: accuracy is required, but Standard 1.1 also bars statements that mislead. This one is chosen so the clerk believes the supervisor explained the losses.
wrong_explanations.D: Standard 1.1's duty to disclose material facts protects the organization's decisions. It does not make an auditor tell an interviewee everything; the fault here is the deception.

tips: Eliminate: A, because the plan is to plant a belief, not to hold facts back, and D, because the duty to disclose material facts concerns the organization's decisions, not an interviewee.
Final two: C beats B because Standard 1.1 bars misleading statements as well as false ones; an accurate remark chosen to create a false belief fails it.
Exam cue: on CIA questions, the internal auditor usually gets to the truth by asking openly and corroborating. An option that relies on a bluff, even an accurate one, loses.

questions.subtopic: 1D5 Fraud investigation techniques and roles. Which forensic task fits the function
questions.question: A forensic firm investigating claims fraud at an insurer seeks help from internal audit. The internal audit charter covers forensic support. The auditors' only forensic training is data analysis. Which request best fits the function?

options.A: Recovering deleted emails from the claims unit's mail server.
options.B: Searching all claim payments for repeated payee bank accounts.
options.C: Imaging the two handlers' laptops so that the data can be analyzed.
options.D: Interviewing the two claims handlers named in the allegation.

questions.key_concept: The mandate says which services the function may give; competency says which tasks it can take. Forensic support is advisory work within both limits.
questions.pre_read: The charter settles whether the function may help. For each request, ask which skill the task needs and whether the auditors have it.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 3.1 lets internal auditors take on only services they have, or can obtain, the competencies for, and the glossary lists forensic services among advisory services. The charter covers the work, so the question is skill. Searching all payments for repeated payee accounts is data analysis. Recovering deleted emails is the runner-up: it also handles data, but it is digital forensics, a separate skill these auditors do not have.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: it looks like data work, but recovering deleted mail is digital forensics, a separate skill. Standard 3.1 keeps the auditors to skills they have or can obtain.
wrong_explanations.C: Imaging a laptop prepares data for analysis, but capturing it from a device is digital forensics. These auditors are trained to analyze data, not to collect it that way.
wrong_explanations.D: Interviewing people named in an allegation is investigative work. The auditors' only forensic training is data analysis, so Standard 3.1 points away from this task.

tips: Eliminate: C, because capturing data from a device is digital forensics and not analysis, and D, because interviewing people named in an allegation needs investigative training.
Final two: B beats A because searching payments for repeated payee accounts is data analysis, while recovering deleted emails is digital forensics the auditors are not trained for.
Exam cue: for a request to help investigators, check the charter, then match each task to a skill the auditors have or can obtain. Take those tasks only.

questions.subtopic: 1D2 Weighing fraud risk in an engagement. Which change since last year raises fraud exposure most
questions.question: An internal auditor is planning an engagement on a rice exporter's four main processes. The processes were found effective last year. Which change since then should most raise the auditor's rating of fraud exposure?

options.A: Supplier spending rose by a third, still under the same tested controls.
options.B: Hotline reports doubled after an awareness drive, and none was upheld.
options.C: Credit notes that needed two approvers now need just one, unreviewed.
options.D: Stock counts moved from yearly to quarterly at management's request.

questions.key_concept: Fraud exposure rises most when a change removes an independent check; growth under controls that still work raises it less.
questions.pre_read: For each change, ask whether it alters who can act alone and unseen, or only how much passes through.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 13.2 requires internal auditors to consider specific fraud risks and to update a past engagement risk assessment; its considerations ask what has changed and weigh impact and likelihood. Dropping the second approver and the review leaves one person's sign-off as the only check on each credit, a jump in opportunity, a fraud triangle condition the syllabus names. Higher spending, the closest choice, raises the stakes under controls found effective.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: more spending raises what is at stake, but controls found effective still cover it. Likelihood barely moves here; in the credit notes it jumps.
wrong_explanations.B: More reports after a campaign often show more trust in the channel. With none upheld, they point to no new exposure; a cluster on one unit would.
wrong_explanations.D: More frequent counts find losses sooner. That strengthens detection and lowers exposure; it would raise the rating only if counts had been dropped.

tips: Eliminate: B, because more reports after a campaign, none upheld, show trust rather than exposure, and D, because more frequent counts strengthen detection.
Final two: C beats A because dropping the second approver and the review leaves one sign-off unchecked; more spending under controls found effective mostly raises the stakes.
Exam cue: on CIA questions, exposure moves most when a change removes an independent check; growth in volume or spending under working controls moves it less.

questions.subtopic: 1D3 Fraud risk management and red flags. Untrained unit heads as investigators
questions.question: A port has a 2021 fraud policy, an outsourced hotline and a response plan in which untrained unit heads investigate their units' reports. Which weakness should an internal auditor rate most significant?

options.A: Response plan: its investigators may spoil evidence or accuse wrongly.
options.B: Policy: not reissued since 2021, so its rules may be outdated.
options.C: Internal audit: the plan gives it no investigative role.
options.D: Hotline: an outside firm cannot judge which reports matter.

questions.key_concept: A fraud response plan should send reports to suitably qualified investigators; untrained investigators put the evidence and fairness of every case at risk.
questions.pre_read: For each feature, ask how many cases it could harm and whether the stem shows an actual gap.
questions.correct_explanation: The IIA's position paper on fraud treats investigation by suitably qualified people as essential, because a badly run inquiry can ruin evidence and wrongly accuse someone. Here every report goes to an untrained unit head, so the flaw reaches every case. The closest choice, an old policy, may need refreshing, but its age alone shows no gap in what it says.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: a policy needs updating when laws or the business change, but age alone shows no gap. The response plan's flaw touches every report now.
wrong_explanations.C: Investigating is not normally internal audit's task. The position paper asks a response plan to make internal audit's part clear, not to make it an investigator.
wrong_explanations.D: An outside firm receives and passes on reports; judging them is the investigators' job. It would be a weakness only if the firm screened reports out.

tips: Eliminate: C, because investigating is not normally internal audit's task, and D, because an outside firm's job is to receive and pass on reports, not to judge them.
Final two: A beats B because the response plan's flaw affects every report now, while the policy's age alone shows no gap in its content.
Exam cue: on CIA questions about fraud programs, weigh who investigates; investigators without the right skills put evidence and fairness at risk in every case.

questions.subtopic: 1D3 Fraud risk management and red flags. Reporting an indicator, not a conclusion
questions.question: An internal auditor at a resort, trained only in financial audit, finds that three suppliers' bank accounts match a clerk's. The methodology sends this to the chief audit executive. What should the report best contain?

options.A: The facts, and that they show the clerk probably committed fraud.
options.B: The matching accounts, rated as a finding for the final report.
options.C: The facts, with the auditor's plan to interview the clerk.
options.D: The matching accounts, and whether to consider an investigation.

questions.key_concept: Internal auditors report fraud indicators as facts and say whether an investigation should be considered; they do not conclude that fraud occurred.
questions.pre_read: Separate what the bank records show from what they might mean, then ask who decides what happens next.
questions.correct_explanation: The IIA's position paper on fraud gives internal auditors the task of weighing fraud indicators and deciding whether further action or an investigation should be recommended; establishing that fraud occurred falls to qualified investigators and those with authority to act. Matching bank accounts are a strong indicator, not proof. The closest choice mistakes honesty for certainty: Standard 1.1 requires accurate communication and no misleading statement.

questions.subtopic: 1D5 Fraud investigation techniques and roles. Complaint trends in the yearly plan
questions.question: A trading firm's investigators tell the chief audit executive that 25 of 60 hotline complaints concern procurement in two regions. Eight remain open. What is the best use of this for next year's plan?

options.A: Leave the complaints to the investigators, whose cases they are.
options.B: Weigh the procurement cluster within the plan's risk assessment.
options.C: Audit procurement in every region, since the complaints point to it.
options.D: Use the complaints in the plan once investigators uphold them.

questions.key_concept: Patterns in whistleblower complaints and investigation trends feed the plan's risk assessment and its fraud coverage; the cases and names stay with investigators.
questions.pre_read: Separate the pattern in the complaints from the cases themselves, and ask which of the two the plan needs.
questions.correct_explanation: The CIA syllabus names whistleblower complaints and investigation trends among the information internal auditors can review with fraud investigators, and Standard 9.4 requires the plan to rest on a documented risk assessment that considers coverage of fraud risk. A cluster of 25 complaints in two regions is such a signal now. The closest choice waits for upheld cases, but the plan weighs exposure, not proof.

wrong_explanations.A: Investigators handle the cases, and details stay confidential. Using the pattern of complaints to plan coverage takes nothing from them and needs no names.
wrong_explanations.C: The complaints cluster in two regions, so that is where they point. A risk-based plan weighs that pattern instead of spreading the work across every region.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: upheld cases confirm fraud, but the plan weighs exposure, not proof. A cluster of complaints signals it now; the open cases need only coordination.

tips: Eliminate: A, because using the pattern of complaints needs no names and takes no case from the investigators, and C, because the cluster points to two regions, not to every region.
Final two: B beats D because the plan's risk assessment weighs exposure, which a cluster of complaints already shows; waiting for upheld cases treats planning input as proof.
Exam cue: on CIA questions, a pattern in complaints or cases tells the plan where fraud exposure sits; the cases themselves and the names stay with the investigators.

questions.subtopic: 1D4 Controls that prevent and detect fraud. Bonuses for targets met however met
questions.question: A telecom's new chief executive pays sales bonuses based only on targets. The controls are unchanged. An audit committee member asks the chief audit executive about fraud risk. Which reply is most accurate?

options.A: Higher: the bonus rule adds pressure to get around unchanged controls.
options.B: Unchanged until tests show the sales controls are being bypassed.
options.C: Higher where sales controls were rated weak, unchanged where strong.
options.D: Lower: bigger bonuses ease the money pressures that lead to theft.

questions.key_concept: Tone at the top changes the likelihood of fraud: leaders who reward results however reached invite misconduct, even when controls stay the same.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the new bonus rule tells staff about how targets may be met, and whether unchanged controls answer that.
questions.correct_explanation: The CIA syllabus ties tone at the top to the likelihood of fraud, and Standard 4.2 has due professional care weigh how probable fraud is. A chief executive who pays on targets alone tells staff that bending rules pays, which feeds pressure and excuses. The closest choice waits for tests, but Standard 9.4 has the plan respond to changes in culture as well as controls, and this signal raises likelihood before any control fails.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: tests show whether controls work, but likelihood is judged from conditions first. The plan must respond to changes in culture, not only in controls (Standard 9.4).
wrong_explanations.C: Weak controls raise risk most, but tone reaches every area. Pressure to hit targets can push people to get around controls rated strong, so likelihood rises there too.
wrong_explanations.D: Fair pay can ease money pressure, but these bonuses reward hitting targets by any method. That adds pressure to cheat instead of removing it.

tips: Eliminate: C, because a weak tone raises fraud likelihood even where controls are strong, and D, because bonuses for results by any method add pressure instead of easing it.
Final two: A beats B because likelihood is judged from conditions such as incentives, and the plan must respond to culture changes; tests come later.
Exam cue: on CIA questions, a leader's signal that results matter more than how they are reached raises the likelihood of fraud, even with controls unchanged.

questions.subtopic: 1D4 Controls that prevent and detect fraud. An approval limit the payment system does not enforce
questions.question: A fishing company's policy requires manager approval for payments over $10,000. But the payment system lets clerks release any payment, and no one reviews releases. How should an internal auditor best assess the limit's design?

options.A: Sound: the policy puts approval before release, which prevents fraud.
options.B: Sound, though its operation needs testing on a sample of payments.
options.C: Mis-set: the $10,000 threshold is too high for payments of this kind.
options.D: Weak: a clerk intent on fraud can release payments around it unseen.

questions.key_concept: An authority level prevents fraud only if a payment cannot proceed, or pass unnoticed, without approval; a limit clerks skip unseen is weak in design.
questions.pre_read: Ask what actually stops a clerk from releasing a large payment without the manager's approval.
questions.correct_explanation: The glossary treats control processes as designed and operated to keep risk within tolerance, and the syllabus says authority levels may prevent fraud. Here nothing stops or catches a release without the manager, so a clerk who means to commit fraud can skip the approval unseen: the design cannot manage that risk. The closest choice reads the written rule as the control; a rule nothing enforces or checks is intent, not prevention.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the written rule is preventive in intent, but nothing makes a clerk follow it. A limit that the person it restrains can ignore cannot stop that person.
wrong_explanations.B: Testing operation suits a sound design. Here the design itself lets payments bypass approval, so clean samples would show only that clerks chose to comply.
wrong_explanations.C: Nothing in the stem suggests the amount is wrong. Lowering the threshold would not help while clerks can still release any payment unreviewed.

tips: Eliminate: B, because sampling clean payments cannot repair a design that lets approval be skipped, and C, because no fact suggests the amount is wrong.
Final two: D beats A because a limit prevents fraud only if the payment must wait for approval or a skip is caught; a written rule alone does not stop a determined clerk.
Exam cue: on CIA questions, an approval limit is preventive only if something makes the transaction wait for it or catches a skip; check what does.
